\chapter{The Heart, Two Ways}
\label{ch:te-heart}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my heart in Telugu two ways, the everyday native word and the literary Sanskrit loan, and trace the Sanskrit one to the same Proto-Indo-European root as the English word heart.}

Say \te{నా} \te{గుండె} and \te{నా} \te{హృదయం} \te{నీది}, set the everyday native word beside the literary Sanskrit loan, and trace \te{హృదయం} to the same PIE root as English heart, Latin cor and Greek kardía.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[guṇḍe]{\te{గుండె} (guṇḍe) — \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} the everyday native word}

\label{lesson:TE-C38-gunde}



\begin{quote}
Four face words done, one of them an honest gap. This chapter gives you a fifth body word — and then, unusually, a second word for the very same thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గుండె}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{గుండె}} — \emph{guṇḍe} — \textbf{heart}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{గుండె}.} — \emph{nā guṇḍe.} — \textquotedblleft{}My heart.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{గుండె}} is inherited from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kuṇṭV}, and it is cognate with Kannada's own native heart-word, \textbf{\ka{ಗುಂಡಿಗೆ}} (\emph{guṇḍige}) — plainly the same root, wearing a different Telugu and Kannada shape. \emph{Guṇḍe} is the plain, physical, everyday word: the organ beating in your chest. The next lesson gives Telugu's \emph{other} word for heart — not a synonym so much as a different register entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā guṇḍe\textquotedblright{} — my heart
  \item the Kannada cognate — \textquotedblleft{}guṇḍe … guṇḍige\textquotedblright{}
  \item five body words — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … cevi … mukku … nōru … guṇḍe\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my heart.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nā guṇḍe}.) Is \emph{guṇḍe} native or borrowed? (\textbf{Native Dravidian}, from Proto-Dravidian \emph{*kuṇṭV}.) Which language carries a matching native heart-word? (\textbf{Kannada}, \emph{guṇḍige}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hṛdayaṁ]{\te{హృదయం} (hṛdayaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} and a genuine cousin of the English word}

\label{lesson:TE-C38-hrudayam}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Guṇḍe} is the heart beating in your chest. This word is the heart Telugu reaches for in a poem, a speech, or a love letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{హృదయం}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{హృదయం}} — \emph{hṛdayaṁ} — \textbf{heart} (literary, emotional register)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{హృదయం} \te{నీది}.} — \emph{nā hṛdayaṁ nīdi.} — \textquotedblleft{}My heart is yours.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{హృ}} is \textbf{\te{హ}} (\emph{ha}) carrying the \textbf{vocalic-r vowel sign} \textbf{\te{ృ}} — the \emph{dependent} form of the same vowel Chapter 14 gave you as the \emph{independent} letter \textbf{\te{ఋ}}, standing alone at the front of \textbf{\te{ఋతువు}}. Same vowel, two shapes: one when it opens a word, another when it rides on a consonant. \textbf{\te{దయం}} closes with the familiar \textbf{\te{అనుస్వార} \te{ం}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{హృదయం}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{हृदय}}, built on \textbf{\dv{हृद्}} (\emph{hṛd}), \textquotedblleft{}heart.\textquotedblright{} That Sanskrit root and the English word \textbf{heart} are not a coincidence of sound — both descend from the same reconstructed Proto-Indo-European root, \textbf{*\'{k}ērd-}. Latin's \textbf{cor} (genitive \emph{cordis}, the source of English \emph{cordial} and \emph{courage}) and Greek's \textbf{kardía} (behind \emph{cardiac}) come from that exact same root. Four languages, one ancient word.

Telugu keeps \emph{hṛdayaṁ} beside native \emph{guṇḍe} the same way Chapter 32 kept Sanskrit \emph{bhōjanaṁ} beside native \emph{tiṇḍi}: the plain, physical word stays Dravidian; the word for ceremony, poetry, and feeling is layered on top from Sanskrit.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā hṛdayaṁ nīdi\textquotedblright{} — my heart is yours
  \item the four cousins — \textquotedblleft{}hṛd … heart … cor … kardía\textquotedblright{}
  \item native, then literary — \textquotedblleft{}guṇḍe … hṛdayaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item all six body words now — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … cevi … mukku … nōru … guṇḍe … hṛdayaṁ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my heart is yours.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nā hṛdayaṁ nīdi}.) Is \emph{hṛdayaṁ} a real Indo-European cousin of English \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} or just a coincidence of sound? (\textbf{A real cousin} — both from PIE \emph{*\'{k}ērd-}, alongside Latin \emph{cor} and Greek \emph{kardía}.) Which is the everyday, physical word for heart, and which is literary? (\textbf{\te{గుండె}} everyday; \textbf{\te{హృదయం}} literary.)
\end{tcolorbox}
